clue.text: English county of French and of German origin

parts.note: de is the French word for 'of'
von is the German word for 'of', found in noble surnames

explanation.surface: A question about which English county has French and German roots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'origin' is a link word: the county's name is built from the French and German words for 'of'. Devon is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Devon is a shire in the south-west of England, between Cornwall and Somerset.

clue.text: For best quality hi-fi, reset "Reset" to zero

indicators.note: to reset something is to set it again in a new arrangement, so the letters of the quoted word are rearranged

parts.note: zero is the figure 0, the letter O

explanation.surface: Advice to a hi-fi owner to set the controls back to zero for best sound.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'reset' is the anagram signal acting on the quoted word 'Reset', giving STERE; O for zero follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-channel sound reproduction gives fuller, more realistic playback than mono, so it is the choice for top-quality audio.

clue.text: Always go into house payments with great solemnity

indicators.note: one word is told to go into the other, so it sits inside it

parts.note: rent is what a tenant pays for a house
ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: Someone paying for a house every month, very solemnly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go into' is the container signal; 'with great solemnity' is an adverbial phrase standing for the adjective, as in 'bowed, reverent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being deeply respectful and solemn, as in a church, is the sense of this adjective.

clue.text: Three months is something Judge Jeffreys would never have given

definitions.text: something Judge Jeffreys would never have given

explanation.surface: A quarter of a year set beside the harshest judge in English history.
explanation.walkthrough: Judge Jeffreys was the 17th-century 'Hanging Judge' of the Bloody Assizes, known for showing no mercy; to give no quarter is to show no mercy.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarter is a fourth of a year, and also mercy shown to a beaten enemy, which the notoriously cruel judge withheld.

clue.text: Faint light is not permitted!

explanation.surface: A weak glimmer of light being banned, as in wartime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faint' looks like an adjective describing the light but is a verb: to lose consciousness. The second sense is the wartime rule that no light may show at night.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose consciousness briefly is to pass out; a wartime order to hide every lamp from bombers was also so called.

clue.text: Drops seen oozing out, yet kept going

indicators.note: liquid oozing out spreads and loses its shape, so these letters are reformed

explanation.surface: Drops leaking from somewhere, but someone carried on regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oozing out' rearranges DROPS and SEEN; 'yet' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To continue determinedly despite difficulty is to push forward.

clue.text: Order round children to get a good start

definitions.text: children to get a good start

explanation.surface: Ordering children around so they get off to a good beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is to buy a round of drinks in a pub; the second is giving children a good start in life.
explanation.definitionFit: To line up drinks for friends at a bar, or to give youngsters a strong footing for their future.

clue.text: Mentally wide awake, but not all clear

explanation.surface: Someone sharp of mind, yet the situation is not entirely clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is wartime: an air-raid warning, the opposite of the 'all clear' siren that ends one.
explanation.definitionFit: Watchful and quick to notice describes the first; a siren warning of attack, before the safety signal, is the second.

clue.text: Sail up to the limestone rock

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the word is taken as written

explanation.surface: A boat sailing up to a limestone crag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the word backwards. Lias is a blue-grey limestone of the early Jurassic, found in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Lias is a geological series of layered blue limestone and shale.

clue.text: Unfortunate person in need, and prices are high

parts.note: poor means lacking money, in need
dear means expensive, costing a lot

explanation.surface: A struggling person facing high prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link word joining the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An expression of sympathy for someone suffering, a pitiable soul.

clue.text: Where counsel may be needed just as a precaution

explanation.surface: Taking a lawyer along to be on the safe side.
explanation.walkthrough: Counsel means a barrister, who works on a legal action, a 'case'.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister is needed during a lawsuit; the phrase also means as a safeguard against something happening.

clue.text: He does keep talking well

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps talking well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well' looks like an adverb praising the talker but is a noun: a drilled hole, as for water or oil.
explanation.definitionFit: A tedious person who drones on; also a borehole sunk into the ground.

clue.text: Make way for passing cars when past the rest

parts.note: ease means rest or relaxation, as in 'at ease'
over means past or finished, as in 'the storm is over'

explanation.surface: A driver pulling aside for traffic once the rest stop is behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorist moves gently to the side so that overtaking vehicles can get by.

clue.text: Irrespective of actual speed whatever else matters

explanation.surface: Never mind how fast you go, whatever else is the case.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads 'rate' as speed; the second is the everyday phrase meaning 'in any case'.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, at whichever velocity; idiomatically, regardless of anything else.

clue.text: He sat on a pillar because it was in the way

indicators.note: one piece is said to be in the other, so it sits inside it

parts.note: style is a way or manner of doing something

explanation.surface: A man perched on a column because something was blocking the path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'because' is a link word and 'was in' the container signal. St Simeon Stylites was the famous early Christian ascetic who lived atop a pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: An early Christian hermit who lived on top of a column as an act of devotion.

clue.text: Now listen! This is where you should be searching

definitions.text: This is where you should be searching

explanation.surface: Someone demanding attention and pointing out where to search.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the phrase literally: search in this spot.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation demanding attention; read literally, an instruction to search at this spot.

clue.text: Where so often one sees a train standing and standing

definitions.text: Where so often one sees a train standing

explanation.surface: A train standing still, as trains so often do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link word. The second sense is social position or rank, as in 'above one's ...'.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway stop where trains wait at platforms; also rank or social status.

clue.text: Try underground experimental equipment

parts.note: to test is to try out
the Tube is the London Underground railway

explanation.surface: Trying out the underground railway.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is the everyday name for London's underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A slim glass cylinder used to hold samples in a laboratory.

clue.text: Proud to have been attacked by a gunman

definitions.text: to have been attacked by a gunman

explanation.surface: Someone feeling proud after being held up by a gunman.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the slang for an armed robbery: 'stick 'em up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Snobbishly arrogant; also robbed at gunpoint in a hold-up.

clue.text: Best place to keep a wallet if one has any money left over

definitions.text: Best place to keep a wallet
if one has any money left over

explanation.surface: Advice on where to carry a wallet when there is cash to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense means having made a profit, being ahead financially.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally inside a pouch in one's clothes; idiomatically, having gained money.

clue.text: Enterprise chief supported by elders

explanation.surface: A business leader backed by senior figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enterprise' looks like a business but is the starship of Star Trek, captained by James T. Kirk. The second sense is the Scottish word for a church, run by elders in the Presbyterian tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain of the starship in Star Trek; also a Scottish church governed by elders.

clue.text: Is he sore with the decision to strike?

definitions.text: Is he sore with the decision to strike?

parts.words: Is he sore with the decision to strike?
parts.note: one reading is a crust that forms on a wound; the other is a worker who is angry with colleagues' vote to walk out and so carries on working

explanation.surface: A worker unhappy about his union voting to strike.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both the crust over a sore and a strikebreaker, a worker who refuses to join a strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A crust over a healing wound, and the insulting name for a worker who crosses a picket line.

clue.text: The habit of a sober man surmounting anger

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece surmounting another sits on top of it

parts.note: TT is short for teetotal, a person who never drinks

explanation.surface: A teetotaller keeping his temper in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surmounting' puts A and TT above IRE in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is clothing, as a monk's robe, and so is dress in general.

clue.text: Copper embarrassed, but now free of ill-feeling

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
an embarrassed person goes red in the face

explanation.surface: A policeman blushing, but no longer holding a grudge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal; 'ill-feeling' reads as resentment but means illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Healed of a sickness, no longer unwell.

clue.text: One who takes the bow in a radio drama

explanation.surface: An actor taking a bow in a radio play.
explanation.walkthrough: The bow is the weapon, not a gesture to the audience. The Archers is a long-running BBC radio soap about a farming family.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowman shoots arrows; also a member of the family in Britain's longest-running radio soap.

clue.text: Stop advising a reader to keep a news clipping

definitions.text: advising a reader to keep a news clipping

explanation.surface: Telling a newspaper reader to save an article.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: scissor the item from the page.
explanation.definitionFit: A curt order to quit doing something; literally, snip the article from the newspaper.

clue.text: Begin to jump

explanation.surface: Beginning to jump.
explanation.definitionFit: To commence; also to flinch suddenly in surprise.

clue.text: The decimal basis to which most ambitious MPs aspire

definitions.text: to which most ambitious MPs aspire

explanation.surface: The base of our counting system and the goal of every ambitious politician.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is 10 Downing Street, the Prime Minister's official London home.
explanation.definitionFit: Decimal counting works in base ten; the Prime Minister lives at that address in Downing Street.
